title: How the Phone Changed Everyday Life
summary: Once telephones reached shops, farms and homes, life sped up. Farmers strung phone lines along their fences, people could call for help with three simple numbers, and deaf people found a clever way to 'talk' by typing over the phone.

sections.heading: The Office That Never Stopped Ringing
paragraphs: Picture a busy shop counter in an American city around 1885. Behind the counter, bolted to the wall, is a wooden box with a crank on the side and a little horn to speak into. When it rings, the shopkeeper hurries over, lifts the earpiece and hears a customer from across town asking for two pounds of coffee and a sack of flour to be delivered before supper. Ten years earlier, that order would have needed a walk, a horse ride or a messenger boy. Now it took less than a minute.

The very first people to rent telephones were mostly not families. They were businesses: doctors, pharmacies, hotels, factories, banks, newspapers, livery stables that rented out horses, and shops of every kind. For them, the telephone was not a fun gadget. It was a tool that saved time, and in business, time is money. A factory owner could call a supplier to ask whether a shipment of iron had left the station. A doctor could be called to a sick child's bedside without someone running through the streets to find him.

Money markets changed too. Traders had already used the telegraph and the ticker tape machine, which printed share prices on long paper strips. The telephone added something new: a real conversation. A broker could talk to a client, hear the worry or excitement in their voice, ask a question and get an answer straight away. Over the following decades, trading floors filled with telephones, and shouting into a receiver became part of the noisy music of every stock exchange.

Newspapers loved the telephone. A reporter standing at the scene of a fire or a big court case no longer had to rush back to the office. He or she could find the nearest phone and read the story out loud to a 'rewrite' desk, where another journalist typed it up for the next edition. That meant news reached readers hours sooner. Big stores began taking orders by phone, and catalogue companies and grocers built whole delivery systems around the ring of a bell.

There was a quieter change, too. Before the telephone, important business was usually done face to face or by letter. Now deals could be made, cancelled or changed in a single call. Offices began to hire people whose main job was answering the phone politely and passing on messages. The 'telephone voice' — a slightly brighter, clearer way of speaking used on calls — became part of office life. By the early 1900s, a company without a telephone number printed on its letters and adverts looked old-fashioned.

sections.heading: Farmers, Fences and the Ring for Everyone
paragraphs: In the countryside, the story was different and, in some ways, more surprising. Big telephone companies wanted to build lines where lots of customers lived close together, because that brought the most money for each kilometre of wire. A farmhouse kilometres from its nearest neighbour was not very tempting. For years, many farm families were left out.

Then came an important date. Alexander Graham Bell's two key telephone patents expired in 1893 and 1894. Once they ran out, anyone was allowed to build and sell telephones. Thousands of small 'independent' telephone companies sprang up across the United States, especially in the Midwest. Some were run by local businesspeople. Many were owned by the farmers themselves, who formed 'mutual' or co-operative companies: each family paid a share, helped put up the poles and wire, and took turns keeping the line in repair.

Some farmers found an even cheaper trick. Around the turn of the twentieth century, in some rural areas, people used the barbed-wire fences that already stretched between their fields as telephone lines. A metal fence is a long piece of wire, after all, and electricity does not care whether the wire has sharp barbs on it. Families connected a telephone to the top strand of fence, sometimes with short bits of wire to jump across gates and roads. These fence lines were crackly, and they could stop working when wet weeds or a fallen post touched the wire, but they cost almost nothing and could link a whole valley of ranches.

Most rural phones were on party lines, which means one line shared by many homes. Every house on the line heard every ring, so each family had its own pattern, such as two long rings and one short. If it was not your ring, you were supposed to ignore it. (Many people did not, as we will see in the next part.) There was also a special 'general ring', often one very long ring, that meant everyone should pick up. The operator or a neighbour might use it to announce a fire, a storm coming, a lost child, the result of an election, or the weather forecast for farmers about to cut their hay.

For lonely farm families, especially women who might not see another adult for days, the party line became a kind of village square made of wire. People shared recipes, prices for corn and hogs, news of births and illnesses, and warnings about wolves or floods. Some historians point out that, in the early 1900s, farm families in parts of the Midwest were actually more likely to have a telephone than many families in big cities. It is a good reminder that inventions do not just flow down from big companies; ordinary people often grab them and build their own networks.

sections.heading: Nine, Nine, Nine: London Invents the Emergency Number
paragraphs: Travel back to London in November 1935. A fire breaks out at number 27 Wimpole Street, a building where an ear surgeon, Dr Philip Franklin, had his surgery. A neighbour sees the flames and picks up the phone to call the fire brigade. In those days you dialled 0 for the operator and waited. But the exchange was busy, and the call sat in a queue with everybody else's ordinary calls. Five women died in the fire. At the official inquiry afterwards, people learned something shocking: the fire engines had actually arrived before the operator answered the neighbour's call.

The government set up a group of experts, called the Belgrave Committee, to solve a simple but important problem: how could an operator tell, instantly, that a call was an emergency? Their answer was to create one special number, the same everywhere, that anybody could remember even when frightened.

Choosing the number was trickier than you might think. One idea was 707, because on the old dial those numbers lined up with the letters S, O and S, the famous distress signal. Another was 333. But the telephone equipment of the time could not easily handle them. The number had to be three digits to work in London's system, and it had to be dialled from coin-operated phone boxes without putting money in. The number 111 was rejected partly because of a strange technical problem: when wind made overhead wires swing and touch, the tiny clicks could look to the exchange like someone dialling 1-1-1, which would have caused false alarms. So 999 was chosen as the most practical option.

The world's first emergency telephone number went live in London on 30 June 1937, across 91 automatic exchanges. When someone dialled 999, a red light flashed and a loud alarm sounded at the exchange so the operator knew to drop everything. If every operator was busy, one would cut off an ordinary call to take the emergency. The alarm horns were so noisy that, according to one popular telephone-company story, an operator stuffed a tennis ball into one to make it bearable.

In the first week there were 1,336 calls to 999. Most, 1,073, were real emergencies. Some came from people who just wanted the operator, and 91 were listed as coming from practical jokers — a problem emergency services still face today. Within days, a call from a woman in Hampstead led police to arrest a burglar. Glasgow became the second city with 999 in 1938, but the Second World War slowed the spread, and it took years more before the whole country was covered. Today, 999 calls in the UK are counted in the tens of millions every year.

sections.heading: A Red Phone in Haleyville
paragraphs: Across the Atlantic, the United States took much longer to get a single emergency number. For decades, if your house was on fire you had to know the fire station's own number, or dial the operator and hope she could connect you quickly. Every town had different numbers for police, fire and ambulance. Visitors, children and panicking people often had no idea what to dial.

People had been asking for a better system for years. In 1957 the National Association of Fire Chiefs recommended a single number for reporting fires. In 1967 a commission set up by the President to study law enforcement recommended one nationwide emergency number. Late that year, the Federal Communications Commission, the government agency in charge of telephones, met with AT&T, the giant company that ran most of America's phones, to pick it.

Why not copy Britain's 999? On American switching equipment it was not practical. Instead, engineers chose 9-1-1. It was short, it was easy to remember, and it had never been given out as an area code or the start of an ordinary number, so it would not clash with anyone's existing phone number.

AT&T planned to switch on its first 911 system in Huntington, Indiana. But a small, independent company beat it. B. W. Gallagher, the president of the Alabama Telephone Company, read about the plan and decided his company should be first. He chose the little town of Haleyville, Alabama, because its exchange equipment could be changed quickly, and an engineer named Robert Fitzgerald designed and installed the system in less than a week.

On February 16, 1968, Alabama's Speaker of the House, Rankin Fite, picked up a phone and dialled 9-1-1. At the other end, in the Haleyville police station, a bright red phone rang, and US Congressman Tom Bevill answered. It was a ceremonial call — there was no real emergency — but it was the first 911 call in the United States. Huntington, Indiana, got AT&T's own 911 system on March 1, 1968.

Spreading the number across a huge country took a long time, because every local phone system and emergency service had to be changed. About 26 percent of Americans could dial 911 in 1979. By 1987 it was about half, and by 2000 about 93 percent. Later 'Enhanced 911' systems added something brilliant: the dispatcher's screen could show the caller's phone number and address automatically, so help could be sent even if the caller could not speak. Today 911 centres in the US handle roughly 240 million calls a year. Meanwhile, much of Europe adopted another number, 112, as a shared emergency number in 1991, so a traveller can dial the same three digits in many countries.

sections.heading: Number, Please: A Giant Job for Women
paragraphs: Back in Part 11 we met Emma Nutt, who in 1878 became the first woman telephone operator. What started with one young woman in Boston grew into one of the biggest kinds of work open to women anywhere. By the early and middle 1900s, hundreds of thousands of women in the United States alone sat in long rows at switchboards, wearing headsets and plugging cords into jacks while saying 'Number, please?' many hundreds of times a day.

Why women? Telephone companies said women were more polite and patient than the rowdy teenage boys who had first done the job. There was also a less flattering reason: companies could pay women far less. One estimate is that women operators were paid between a quarter and a half of what a man might earn in similar work. Still, for many young women, especially daughters of working families and immigrants, being an operator was a respectable, steady job in a modern industry, and a step away from factory work or cleaning in other people's houses.

The work was hard. Supervisors walked up and down behind the operators, timing how fast they answered. Operators had to use exact, polite phrases, could not chat with callers, and sometimes needed permission to leave their seats. Long shifts with the constant buzz of voices left many exhausted. In 1919 thousands of operators in New England, led by a young union leader named Julia O'Connor, went on strike. After five days, the government agreed to step in, and the operators won higher pay and the right to bargain together as a union.

Operators did far more than connect calls. In small towns, the local operator often knew everyone. People called her to ask the time, to find out where the fire was, to check on the doctor, or to wake them up in the morning. During floods, fires and storms, operators sometimes stayed at their switchboards for hours, calling families one by one to warn them, even when their own homes were in danger.

As automatic dialling spread (Part 12), the number of operator jobs slowly fell. The change was not instant. In the tiny town of Bryant Pond, Maine, people kept using a hand-crank switchboard until 1983. A study published in 2024 by economists James Feigenbaum and Daniel Gross found that older operators who lost their jobs to automation often had a hard time afterwards, but young women in general found work in other growing jobs, such as offices. It is a pattern we still see today: new machines remove some kinds of work and create others.

sections.heading: Party Lines, Long Talks and Calling Grandma
paragraphs: For a long time, a home telephone was something of a luxury. By around 1946, about half of American households had one, and that share kept rising through the 1950s and 1960s. In Britain and many other countries, home phones spread more slowly; plenty of families relied on the red public phone box down the street.

Where was the family phone? Usually in one fixed spot: the hallway, the kitchen wall, or a little table near the front door. Some families even bought a 'telephone seat', a small bench with a shelf for the phone and the thick phone book. The cord was short, so whoever was talking stood or sat right there, in full hearing of everyone walking past. Later, families stretched extra-long curly cords so a teenager could drag the receiver around a corner or into a cupboard for a bit of privacy.

Teenagers and the telephone became a famous pair. From the 1940s onward, newspapers, cartoons and films joked about teens tying up the family line for hours, chatting about school, music and friends. Parents complained that nobody else could get through. Some families paid for a second line just so the grown-ups could make calls.

Long-distance calls were special events. They cost much more than local calls, often charged by the minute, so people kept them short and planned them carefully. Many families waited for evenings or weekends, when the rates were cheaper, to call grandparents in another city. Hearing the voice of a relative hundreds of kilometres away could be so exciting that the whole family crowded around to take turns saying a few words. For soldiers far from home, emigrants who had moved to a new country, and students away at college, the phone call home became an important ritual.

With all this talking came rules of 'phone etiquette'. Books and telephone companies taught people to answer clearly, often with their family name or phone number, to speak at a normal volume, not to shout, and not to call too early in the morning or too late at night. On party lines, good manners meant hanging up if you picked up during someone else's call, and keeping calls short so neighbours could use the line. Children were taught how to take a message with a pencil and notepad kept by the phone. The phone book, listing almost everyone's name, address and number, became a kind of map of the community.

sections.heading: Typing Down the Telephone: Robert Weitbrecht's Clever Coupler
paragraphs: There is a sad twist in the telephone story. Bell spent much of his life working with deaf people, yet for nearly ninety years the telephone itself was almost useless to them. If you cannot hear the voice at the other end, a phone is just a plastic object on the wall. Deaf people had to ask hearing friends or family to make calls for them, or travel in person to deliver even small messages.

The person who changed that was Robert Weitbrecht. He was born deaf in Orange, California, on April 11, 1920. As a teenager he earned a licence for Morse code and became a keen amateur radio operator, chatting by code with people far away. He studied astronomy at the University of California, Berkeley, worked on electronics during the Second World War, and later earned another degree in astronomy from the University of Chicago. In 1957 he went to work at the Stanford Research Institute in California, designing equipment for Lick Observatory.

In 1950 Weitbrecht bought an old teletypewriter, or TTY, from a Los Angeles newspaper plant. A teletypewriter is a machine that looks like a big, heavy typewriter: what you type at one machine is sent as electrical signals and printed out at another. Newspapers and news agencies used them to receive stories. But Weitbrecht's machine could only receive, so he rebuilt it, using clever home-made fixes, so it could send too.

The big problem was connecting TTYs to the telephone network. At the time, the phone company did not want customers wiring their own machines into its lines. Then, in 1964, a deaf orthodontist in Pasadena named Dr James C. Marsters sent Weitbrecht a teletypewriter and asked him to find a way for them to communicate. Weitbrecht designed an 'acoustic coupler'. You placed the ordinary telephone handset into two rubber cups. The coupler turned the TTY's signals into beeping tones, which it played into the phone's mouthpiece, and listened to tones coming out of the earpiece, turning them back into signals for the printer. Because it only used sound, it did not need to be wired into the phone company's lines.

The first tries were messy, with garbled letters. Then, at last, Weitbrecht's words printed clearly on Marsters's machine: 'Are you printing now? Let's quit for now and gloat over the success.' Deaf people could now 'phone' each other by typing. Weitbrecht, Marsters and another deaf man, Andrew Saks, formed a company to make the couplers, and none of them got rich from it. Deaf volunteers collected old teletypewriters that businesses were throwing away, repaired them, and passed them on to deaf families.

The next step was letting deaf and hearing people talk to each other. Relay services were created, in which a trained operator in the middle reads the typed words aloud to the hearing person and types the spoken reply back. In the United States, the Americans with Disabilities Act of 1990 required telephone companies to provide relay services across the country. Weitbrecht was given an honorary doctorate by Gallaudet University, a university for deaf students, in 1974. He died in 1983, but the idea he started grew into today's text relay, captioned phones and video relay services.

sections.heading: A World Rewired
paragraphs: Step back and look at the century between the 1880s and the 1990s, and you can see how deeply the telephone changed daily life. Businesses moved faster. Farmers who had once been isolated for weeks shared news every day. A frightened child could dial three numbers and reach help. Millions of women earned their own wages, and some of them led strikes that improved working conditions for everyone after them. Families separated by oceans could hear each other laugh. And deaf people, after a long wait, found a way in.

But every powerful invention has a shadow side. A line that lets you talk to your friend can also let someone else listen in. A network run by one giant company can make that company very powerful. And clever people can find ways to trick the system for their own benefit. The telephone, it turned out, also created brand-new problems — and some of them are still ringing today.

deepDive: Historians of technology like to ask a deceptively simple question: who decides what an invention is for? The telephone's makers originally imagined it mostly as a business tool. Early Bell System advertising stressed efficiency, and some managers were even uneasy about 'frivolous' social chatter clogging the lines. Sociologist Claude Fischer, in his book America Calling, showed that ordinary users, especially women and rural families, pushed the telephone toward sociability: visiting, gossip, keeping families together. Companies eventually followed, and by the 1920s and 1930s their adverts encouraged people to call friends and relatives. Rural telephony is a striking case. After Bell's basic patents expired in 1893–1894, thousands of independent and farmer-owned companies spread service into the countryside, and for a time the Bell System faced real competition. Many independents later connected to, or were absorbed by, the Bell network after AT&T agreed in 1913 to let them interconnect. Emergency numbers show how engineering details shape policy. Britain picked 999 partly because of how its step-by-step switches counted dialling pulses; 111 was rejected because swinging overhead wires could create accidental pulses. In the US, 911 was chosen because it did not clash with any area code or exchange prefix. Rolling it out took decades because emergency answering is run by local governments, not one national agency: only about 26 percent of Americans could dial 911 in 1979, roughly half by 1987. The 2024 study by James Feigenbaum and Daniel Gross on operator automation is a good example of modern economic history. Using census records, it found that incumbent operators suffered lasting losses, but later generations of young women were not shut out of work, because growing clerical and service jobs absorbed them. Finally, TTY history shows how disabled people often drive their own technology. Weitbrecht's acoustic coupler sidestepped AT&T's restrictions on attached equipment by using sound, and deaf volunteers built the early network themselves from cast-off machines. National relay services followed under the Americans with Disabilities Act of 1990.
funFact: Britain rejected 111 as its emergency number partly because overhead telephone wires swinging together in the wind could accidentally 'dial' 1-1-1.
